original_question: Does the gene associated with Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome (PLS) catalyze the excision of dipeptides from the C-terminus of proteins and peptides?

final_qi.question: Does the gene associated with Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome (PLS) catalyze the excision of dipeptides from the C-terminus of proteins and peptides?
final_qi.long_answer: Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CTSC gene, which encodes the lysosomal cysteine protease cathepsin C (also called dipeptidyl-peptidase I). Cathepsin C is an exopeptidase that sequentially removes dipeptides from the free N-terminus of proteins and peptides. Its enzymatic activity is therefore N-terminal dipeptidyl peptidase activity, not C-terminal cleavage. Because the gene product does not excise dipeptides from the C-terminus, the statement is incorrect.
